abstract:
Proteins are built from domains, and the order of domains along a protein can be read like a sentence. We take every run of three consecutive Pfam domains (a domain trigram) and classify it by its pattern of repetition: all three the same (AAA), the first two (AAB), the last two (ABB), the outer two (ABA) or all different (ABC). We ask whether the proportions of these five patterns are conserved across the chromosomes of a genome and across genomes.
  We built a reproducible workflow and applied it to the UniProt reference proteomes of 16 organisms, from Escherichia coli to human, with Pfam 39.0. In Drosophila melanogaster, 3,107 distinct trigrams split into 63% ABC, 13% each of AAB and ABB, and 5% each of AAA and ABA. Every chromosome arm closely matches this pie: each lies within the range expected for a random set of genes of the same size. The human pie has less ABC (55%) and more AAB and ABB (18% each), and 23 of its 25 chromosomes and other components fall within the random-gene range. Pies of trigram occurrences vary more, mostly because of a few giant repeat proteins.
  Across 199 chromosomes and other proteome components of 14 organisms, tested with a gene-level permutation, 4 (2%) differ from their own proteome in distinct trigrams and 10 (5%) in occurrences, chiefly human and macaque chromosome 19, whose KRAB zinc-finger clusters make it rich in AAA repeats. Across organisms, the distinct-trigram pie is closely conserved among multicellular eukaryotes (ABC 55-67%, with AAB and ABB always within 2 percentage points of each other) and shifts towards ABC in yeasts (75-77%) and bacteria (82-86%).
  The proportion of domain-repetition patterns is therefore conserved across the chromosomes of a genome and shared by plants and animals, while repeat-rich giant proteins and tandem gene clusters account for most of the local deviations.
